components.description:

It is carried in the component and flagged rather than snapped. (2) The paddings are raw numbers on the Figma side too — only itemSpacing is bound to gap/2xs. Binding 4 -> gap/2xs and 8 -> gap/xs would leave 6px as the only gap. (3) Figma hugs the chip around padding + content and draws the 2px stroke inside that padding, so the CSS gives the border back on each inset; the label lands at 8px and the x at 6px, as drawn. components.name: Tags Input
components.description:

Props: Label → label (required — it names the input); State=Focus is Ark's own data-focus on the control, not a prop and not :focus-within — the machine already tracks whether the field owns focus, which keeps the ring steady while focus moves between the entry and a highlighted chip. Reuse this component — do not regenerate it. DESIGNER NOTES: (1) DEPARTURE — the control is drawn fixed at 360. Implemented fluid (100% of its container), like every other Steelbook field. Confirm or overrule. (2) Ark drops the placeholder as soon as a tag exists; the Default frame draws it alongside three, so the placeholder is set on the entry directly to override that. (3) No highlighted chip is drawn. Backspace on an empty entry selects the last tag (Ark sets data-highlighted) before a second Backspace removes it, and right now it looks like any other chip — worth drawing. Rather than invent a skin the editor wears the outline tone, the drawn look for a value not yet committed. Confirm or overrule. (5) No invalid or disabled state is drawn; both are carried from the house tokens (border/danger, bg/disabled) so Ark's data-invalid and data-disabled are not silent. components.name: Tab
components.description:
One tab trigger. Selected is a solid black block — no underline hedging.

CODE: @steelbook/react — Tab (packages/react/src/tabs).
Label -> children. value keys the trigger to its panel.

Selected -> the tabs’ value, never a prop on the trigger.
Interaction -> a skin: Hover is :hover, Disabled is the disabled prop, which Ark forwards to the button.

Selected outranks both. All three Selected=True variants are drawn identically — a selected tab neither lightens on hover nor greys out when disabled — so the selected skin is written last and the hover skin is scoped away from it. Worth stating plainly because the obvious CSS gets this wrong: :hover:enabled outranks [data-selected] on specificity, not source order, and a selected tab would turn grey under the pointer.

Not drawn: Focus. The trigger is a button, so it takes the house 3px orange ring, inset — the tabs sit flush against each other and against the rule, and an outside ring would land on both.

No gaps to close: 40 is size/control-md, 16 is gap/md, and every fill and label colour is bound. This is the cleanest component in the file so far.

components.name: Tabs
components.description:
Tab list over a 3px rule with a content slot below. Selected tab is a black block. Ark UI: Tabs.

CODE: @steelbook/react — Tabs, TabList, TabPanel (packages/react/src/tabs).
Figma draws the list and the panel as frames rather than components, but Ark needs both as elements, so both are surfaced: TabList is the strip, TabPanel is the slot. Every visible state belongs to the Tab triggers inside.

Ark’s Indicator is deliberately not rendered — it is a sliding block that marks the selection, and this design marks it by inverting the tab itself. The description is explicit: no underline hedging.

One thing the file says that a border cannot: the list’s 3px rule is an INSIDE stroke, so it paints over the bottom 3px of the tabs and the strip measures 40, not 43. In code it is a pseudo-element pinned to the bottom of the list, which keeps both facts true — a hovered tab’s grey fill stops at the rule instead of covering it.

Not drawn, and therefore left as-is:
• The 560px width — fluid in code, as with every other content-width component here.
• What happens when there are more tabs than room. The strip clips and the tabs do not shrink, which is what the frame does. If a list can overflow, it needs somewhere to scroll — say so and it will be built.

Nothing loose here: every length and colour in this component is bound to a variable. The root’s white fill is switched off in the file, so the strip is transparent and the panel carries bg/surface.

components.name: Accordion Item

Body.defaultValue: Two colors, one accent, a 4px grid and an unreasonable amount of conviction. Every token in this answer is bound — flip the mode and it holds.

components.description:
One question per 3px rule. Chevron flips when open. Stack items to build an accordion.

CODE: @steelbook/react — AccordionItem (packages/react/src/accordion).
Title -> title. Body -> children. value keys the row.

Expanded -> the accordion’s value, never a prop on the row.
Interaction -> a skin: Hover is :hover, Disabled is the disabled prop, which Ark forwards to the trigger button.

Two decisions the design did not make:
• Hover is painted on the trigger, not the row. Figma fills the row, but only draws Hover closed — where the trigger is the row to the pixel. Flooding an open row would put the answer text on a grey field, which nothing draws.
• Focus is undrawn. The trigger is a button, so it takes the house 3px orange ring, inset — an outside ring would sit on the rule above the row.

Also undrawn: the open/close transition. Nothing animates; the panel is shown and hidden.

Only four of the six axis combinations exist — neither Hover nor Disabled is drawn open. The code holds in all six.

Gaps to close in Figma:
• the 18px chevron sits between size/icon-sm (16) and size/icon-md (20) — the same sub-16 rungs Toast, File Upload, Tag and Signature Pad already need.
• the 20px trigger inset is space/5 and the 24px content inset is space/6 (gap/lg), both exact rungs, but neither is bound to a variable — bind them.
• the 3px rule is stroke/heavy and the fills are all bound; nothing else is loose here.

THE MACHINE LIVES OUTSIDE THE COMPONENT. useTour() is what you hold and
call start(), next(), prev(), setStep(id) on; <Tour> only renders it.
That split is Ark's own Root API and the one Toaster already uses.

step-counter -> nothing. Ark counts the steps and writes the text.
title -> step.title
body -> step.description
Back / Next -> step.actions, default [{ Back, prev }, { Next, next }]
close -> always there; Ark names it "close tour"
className -> appended after the mark's own class, on the drawn box
No children: the mark is fully drawn, so nothing composes into it.

Ark's own switches reach it through the hook (closeOnEscape,
closeOnInteractOutside, keyboardNavigation, preventInteraction,
spotlightOffset, spotlightRadius, onStepChange, onStatusChange,
translations). Stepping, positioning, scroll-into-view, the arrow keys
and the ARIA are Ark's.

THE SPOTLIGHT IS ONE ELEMENT, NOT FOUR. Example / Tour spotlight builds
the dim out of four rectangles around a hole, because that is how a
cut-out is drawn here. Ark cuts the same hole with one clip-path on a
single backdrop, computed from the target's rect, and puts the accent
ring on a second element sized to the target. Same picture, and it
follows a target that moves or scrolls.

Three of Ark's defaults were changed to match what is drawn: the
spotlight sits flush on its target (Ark inflates it by 10 on each
axis), it is square (Ark rounds it by 4), and the counter reads 2 / 5
rather than Ark's 2 of 5.

Implemented as drawn, measured live: mark 320 x 203, 16 inset, 12 gaps,
2px border/default, radius/control, shadow/hard-md at 6/6. Header
288 x 16 at 16,16 — counter at x16 in mono/overline 700 12/14.4 on
text/accent, uppercase; close 16 square at x288. Title at 16,44 in
heading/4 700 20/26 Archivo on text/primary. Body at 16,82 in body/sm
14/20.3 on text/secondary. Actions at 16,155 — Back ghost at x16,
disabled on the first step, Next primary flush right at x254. The
spotlight rect lands exactly on the target rect, 200 x 80 at 79,99,
with the 3px border/accent ring drawn inside it. Backdrop is
bg/overlay. Both modes checked: the mark inverts to bg/surface-raised
gray-900 with a white border and a white slab shadow, and the counter
picks up the dark text/accent.

The mark reads role="alertdialog" with its title and body wired to it,
the close and the two actions are named, and the arrow keys, Escape and
click-outside all end or step the tour.

FOR THE DESIGNER — five things:

1. NOTHING IS DRAWN FOR FINISHING THE TOUR. Ark disables Next on the
   last step, so as drawn a tour ends only through the close in the
   corner, Escape, or a click outside — there is no button that says
   the tour is over. Code leaves it that way rather than inventing one,
   and a last step can opt in by naming its own actions. Should Next
   read DONE or FINISH on the last step? If so it belongs in this file
   as a property or a second variant, and it becomes the default.

2. THE TITLE IS DRAWN IN CAPS AND heading/4 CARRIES NO -transform.
   So the caps are in the content, and every caller has to shout their
   own title. Same question already open on heading/2: if headings in
   this system are always uppercase, the text style should say so and
   the CSS picks it up for free. Until then the stories type the caps.

3. THE 320 WIDTH IS OFF THE SCALE and bound to nothing. Carried as a
   local value and flagged rather than snapped. It is also fixed, so a
   long title wraps rather than widening the mark — which is right for
   a coach mark, but say if it should have a max instead.

4. WHICH ACTION IS PRIMARY, AND WHERE IT SITS, HAD TO BE GENERALISED.
   The frame draws exactly two actions, Back ghost and Next primary,
   sprung apart by a filled spacer. Code reads that as: the LAST action
   is the primary one, and it is pushed to the far edge. That degrades
   correctly — three actions group at the left with one primary at the
   right, a lone action still sits at the right. If a step with three
   actions should look different, draw it.

5. THE SPOTLIGHT RING IS THE SAME ORANGE IN BOTH MODES.
   border/accent resolves to orange/500 with no dark override, unlike
   text/accent, which lifts to orange/400. On the dark canvas the ring
   is the one accent that does not lift. Intentional, or a missing
   override?

ALSO — two system gaps this component ran into:

- No z-index scale. Ark stacks backdrop, spotlight and mark by adding
  to a --tour-z-index custom property, so it has to be declared for the
  sum to resolve. There is nothing in the token set to anchor it to; it
  is set to 0 and the three layers stay relative to one another.
- Ark sizes the backdrop's cut in document coordinates but draws it on
  a viewport-sized box, so on a page taller than one screen the dim
  stops short. The page height is measured in code and handed to the
  stylesheet. Nothing to decide here — noted so it is not mistaken for
  a design choice.

AND: no arrow. Ark can draw one between the mark and its target; this
file draws none, so none is rendered.

components.name: Carousel
components.description:
Slide viewport with peeking neighbors, block nav riding the edges, and square indicators — active stretches orange. Ark UI: Carousel.

CODE: <Carousel label="Product photography" slides={slides} />
  from @steelbook/react — packages/react/src/carousel/Carousel.tsx

slide -> one entry in slides, in order. Ark counts them and derives the
  pages, the snap points and the indicator row from the count.
label -> the region's accessible name. REQUIRED — Ark makes the root a
  region landmark with a roledescription of "carousel", which tells a
  screen reader user the shape of the thing but nothing about what is
  in it. Same rule Marquee already carries.
prev / next -> nothing. Always there; Ark names them "Previous slide"
  and "Next slide", and disables each at its end of the run.
indicators -> nothing. One dot per PAGE, not per slide: at
  slidesPerPage 2 a ten-slide carousel has five of them.
className -> appended after the carousel's own class, on the drawn box
No children: the slides are the content, and Ark ids each one by index.

Ark's own switches pass through (slidesPerPage, slidesPerMove, spacing,
padding, loop, page / defaultPage, autoplay, allowMouseDrag, snapType,
autoSize, inViewThreshold, onPageChange, onDragStatusChange,
translations). The scrolling, snapping, paging maths, keyboard and ARIA
are Ark's.

THE GEOMETRY IS THREE NUMBERS. slidesPerPage 1, 20 between slides, and
a 40 gutter are all that is needed to reproduce this frame. Ark sizes
each slide as 100% of what is left after the gutters — the drawn 480 in
a 560 viewport — and the 18 of each neighbour that shows on either side
falls out of the same arithmetic rather than being placed. Change any
of the three and everything follows: at slidesPerPage 2 the slides
measure 230 and six of them make three dots, which is checked.

Implemented as drawn, measured live: root 560 wide, viewport 560 x 320
on bg/muted with a 2px border/default, gutters 38 inline and 18 block —
the drawn 40 and 20, less the stroke they are measured through. Slides
480 x 280 on bg/surface with their own 2px border, 20 apart, the
current one 40 in from the viewport edge. Nav blocks 40 square on
bg/inverse over icon/inverse, centred on the viewport at y 290 and hung
20 outside each edge. Indicator row 96 wide, dots 10 square on bg/muted
with a 1.5 border/default, the current one 24 wide on bg/accent, 8
apart. Both modes checked: the viewport lifts to gray-800, the slides
to gray-950, the nav blocks invert to white over black, and the active
dot keeps its orange.

Behaviour checked live: the blocks step and disable at each end, the
dots jump, the indicator row takes the arrow keys, Home and End, the
wheel scrolls it, and with loop the first page steps back to the last.
Off-screen slides carry aria-hidden and the visible one carries
data-inview.

FOR THE DESIGNER — five things:

1. IS THE WHITE SLIDE BOX THE COMPONENT, OR THE DEMO? Each slide frame
   carries bg/surface and a 2px border of its own, distinct from the
   bg/muted viewport behind it. Code ships that as the slide's skin, so
   callers drop content into a drawn box rather than styling one
   themselves. If the box was only there to make the slides legible on
   the canvas — and a photo carousel would cover it entirely — it is
   one rule to remove. Same question that is open on the Splitter's
   muted pane.

2. THE INDICATOR ROW IS 8 LEFT OF CENTRE. The row is 96 wide at x 224,
   so it centres on 272 where the frame centres on 280. Nothing in the
   frame explains the 8, and the row is the same 96 whichever dot is
   active, so it is not a stretch artifact. Code centres it. Say if the
   offset is deliberate.

3. THE FRAME IS 10 TALLER THAN WHAT IS IN IT. Viewport 320, then 20 to
   the indicator row, then 10 of dots, is 350 — the frame is 360. Code
   builds the stack, so it measures 350 and the extra 10 is not carried.
   Say if the row is meant to sit in a fixed 40 band under the viewport
   rather than 20 below it.

4. THE DOTS ARE OFF THE SCALE TWICE OVER. 10 square, where the space
   scale steps 8 to 12; and a 1.5 stroke, where stroke/thin is 1 and
   stroke/default is 2. Both are carried as local values and flagged
   rather than snapped. The half pixel is also the one measurement here
   a 1x display cannot draw — a browser floors a border to whole device
   pixels, so it paints at 1 on a laptop screen and 1.5 on a retina
   one. Worth putting the dot on the scale for that alone.

5. NO STATES ARE DRAWN, and three exist. Ark disables a nav block when
   it has nowhere to go, so both borrow the disabled skin the rest of
   the system uses, the way the Date Picker's nav does. Neither the
   blocks nor the dots have a hover, so none was invented — a black
   block that never answers the pointer is the one that reads oddest.
   And no focus is drawn, so both take the house 3px border/focus ring:
   inset on the 40 blocks, and OUTSIDE the 10 dots, because a 3px inset
   ring on a 10px square leaves 4 and swallows the fill that says which
   page you are on.

ALSO — ONE ORIENTATION SHIPS. Ark can run this vertically. This frame
draws only the horizontal case, and a vertical carousel needs its own
gutters, its own nav placement and its own indicator row, so the prop
is closed rather than shipping a skin nobody drew. Draw it and it opens.

AND: the slide contents are demo content, not part of the component —
the image placeholder and the mono caption. That caption is raw
JetBrains Mono 11 with no text style attached; the stories use mono/sm,
which is 12. If the caption is meant to be part of the slide, it needs
a style.

AND: the active dot stretches from 10 to 24 with no motion drawn, so it
snaps. Say if it should ease.
